name: Marco Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Northfield, a commercial farm owned by an agricultural company. We've got 600 outdoor sows, so pigs living in fields with huts, and 450 hectares of wheat and barley that mostly feeds them. I've got a team of seven. My day starts at half six with the sow records on my phone, the AI flags which sows are due to farrow and which huts need checking, and then I'm out in the paddocks with the lads by seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy making the numbers work: a pig unit is a machine with a thousand moving parts, and I like tuning it. I also run a small drone business on the side, scouting crops for neighbours, which I love because it's new. What wears me down is the pig price, which goes up and down like a fairground ride, and head office phoning when it's down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I use this stuff every day and I was hoping for more. I'd post something like, the tools are useful, use them, but don't wait for magic. At the company managers' meeting I'd still push for better software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. Northfield makes money most years, head office rates me, and my job's solid. The pig price cycle is the only thing that bothers me, and I've lived with that for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the sow records, the grain selling and the drone maps, because it already pays for itself. I'd grow the drone scouting a bit, maybe ten more farms, since it's cheap to run. And otherwise I'd carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by the idea, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the drone business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, about a month's mortgage payments a year after costs. But it's growing, and it's mine. If Northfield ever went wrong, it's a foot in the door somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ingrid think about your appetite for new tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ingrid thinks I'd buy a robot dog if I could justify it as a farm expense. She's a dental hygienist, so she's practical about tools. She keeps me honest about what's a toy and what's a business.

say: I'd say I'm **a bit disappointed**, because I hoped for more.
I'd post that the tools are useful, so **use them**, but don't wait for magic.
think: Northfield **makes money**, head office rates me, and my job is solid.
Only the **pig price cycle** bothers me, and I've lived with that for twenty years.
do: Keep using **AI** for sow records, grain selling and drone maps.
Grow the **drone scouting** by about ten more farms.
feel: **Calm**, and a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: My partner Ingrid thinks I'd buy a robot dog if I could justify it as a farm expense.
fieldNote: Treats AI Plateau as a **letdown**, not a relief.
Job and income feel **secure**; pig prices are the only worry.
His **drone business** is small but a deliberate backup.
**Ingrid** acts as his reality check on spending.

steps.text: Keep using AI for sow records, grain sales and drone maps
Sign up about ten more farms for drone crop scouting
Carry on managing the Northfield pig and grain unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, real progress with time to adapt. I'd say farmers who learn the tools will do well and the ones who don't will struggle. I'd be the one at the managers' meeting saying let's get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's great for me. I'm the guy at Northfield who already knows this stuff, so I'd be the one head office asks to roll it out across their other farms. The risk is that the planning and buying side of my job goes to software and they decide one manager can run two farms, but I'd want to be that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch head office on a trial of autonomous feeders and a robot that checks the farrowing huts, within the year. I'd expand the drone business into spraying, which needs a licence I'd get over the winter. And I'd put some savings into a second drone, roughly two months' pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit hungry, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one manager could run two farms. What happens to the other manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary runs the company's other pig unit up the road. I'd feel bad for Gary (who runs the company's other pig unit), who's 58 and hates computers, but I wouldn't turn the second farm down. That's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your team of seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture robots come slowly, so I'd keep them, maybe lose one through retirement and not replace him. I'd train the younger ones on the new kit. The good stockmen will always have work with me.

say: I'd say this is the **good version**, with real progress and time to adapt.
I'd tell managers that farmers who **learn the tools** will do well.
think: I already know this stuff, so head office would ask me to **roll it out**.
If **one manager** runs two farms, I want to be that one.
do: Pitch head office a trial of **autonomous feeders** and hut-checking robots this year.
Get a **drone spraying licence** over the winter.
Spend about **two months' pay** on a second drone.
feel: **Excited** and a bit hungry for it.
S1.quote: I'd feel bad for Gary (who runs the company's other pig unit), who's 58 and hates computers, but I wouldn't turn the second farm down.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as a **promotion** chance.
Honest that a **colleague's loss** could be his gain.
Puts real **money and time** into the drone business.
Keeps his team but plans **not to replace** retirements.

steps.text: Pitch head office a trial of autonomous feeders and hut-checking robots
Get a drone spraying licence over the winter
Buy a second drone with about two months' pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge opportunity for anyone who moves fast, and a disaster for anyone who doesn't. I'd say governments need to get basic rules in place, because two years is nothing. At the managers' meeting I'd say get the robots booked now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's riskier for me than it looks. My job is half thinking work, the planning, selling grain, managing people, and that goes to AI in 2028. The other half, out with the pigs, goes when the robots arrive around 2031. Head office could run Northfield from a server by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start building savings hard, getting to six months by 2028 instead of spending on toys. I'd move my drone business towards fixing and running farm robots for other farms, because that's where the work will be in that three-year gap. I'd put some savings into a fund that holds robotics and farmland, so I'm on both sides of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but wired. I'd be busy, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be on both sides. Do you think that's enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. A bit of savings in a fund doesn't replace a salary. It just means I'm not only on the losing side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ingrid and the kids notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ingrid would notice I'm up late with the laptop again. Nico's twelve and he'd want to help with the robots, which I'd love. Elsa's nine and she'd just want the pigs to stay.

say: I'd say it's a **huge opportunity** for fast movers and a disaster for others.
I'd call on governments for **basic rules**, because two years is nothing.
think: Half my job is **thinking work** that goes to AI in 2028.
The hands-on half goes with **robots around 2031**, so Northfield could run from a server.
do: Build savings to **six months** by 2028 instead of buying toys.
Turn the drone business towards **running farm robots** for others.
Put savings into a **robotics and farmland fund**.
feel: **Anxious** but wired, busy rather than frozen.
S2.quote: Head office could run Northfield from a server by 2032.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that a **manager's job** is exposed on both fronts.
Uses the **three-year gap** to pivot his side business.
Admits investing is **not a salary**; it just hedges.
Excitement and **anxiety** sit side by side.

steps.text: Build household savings to six months by 2028
Turn the drone business towards running other farms' robots
Put savings into a fund holding robotics and farmland shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the smart farms to get ready. I'd tell neighbours to start trialling things now. I'd post about it, probably a bit too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is plenty for me. Thinking AI in 2031, robots in 2034, I'd be 51 with the kids mostly grown. I could build the robot service business into something real by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get the drone spraying licence, sign up a robot dealer as a partner, and offer a robot setup service to farms around here. I'd push head office to make Northfield the company's test farm, with me running it. And I'd invest a bit of savings in the side business each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a good uneasy. Like before a big sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk to you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the robot companies run their own service and cut out people like me. If they do, I'd still have the Northfield job until 2034. So I'd be fine for a while, just not sure for how long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave Northfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the side business was paying more than my Northfield salary by 2030, I'd leave, with a year's savings behind us. I'd talk to Ingrid first. But yes.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for smart farms to get ready.
I'd tell neighbours to **start trialling** robots now.
think: **Five years** is plenty for me, with the kids mostly grown by 2034.
I could build the **robot service business** into something real.
do: Sign up a **robot dealer** as a partner and offer setup services.
Push head office to make Northfield the **company's test farm**.
Put some **savings** into the side business each year.
feel: **Uneasy**, but a good uneasy, like before a big sale.
S3.quote: If the side business was paying more than my Northfield salary by 2030, I'd leave, with a year's savings behind us.
fieldNote: Five years makes him think like an **entrepreneur**.
Has a clear **exit trigger**: side income beating salary.
Risk he names: **robot makers** cutting out local service.
Still checks big moves with **Ingrid**.

steps.text: Partner with a robot dealer to offer farm robot setup
Push head office to make Northfield its test farm
Put a share of savings into the side business yearly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and anyone who's caught out has only themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh. I'd say plan now and you'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm. I'd be 53 when robots arrive in 2039, and I'd plan to be running my own robot service business well before then. My mortgage would be nearly paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, growing the drone business and testing new tools at Northfield. I'd invest steadily in the side business and some shares. I'd keep learning, because that's the fun bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone caught out only has themselves to blame. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. Gary up the road won't have himself to blame, he's just older and was never shown how. I'd take that back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Nico and Elsa by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Nico and Elsa to have skills a robot can't copy easily, like dealing with people. I'd want my kids to be the ones owning a robot, not competing with one.

say: I'd say **ten years** is generous, so plan now and you'll be fine.
I'd first say people caught out **only have themselves** to blame, then take it back.
think: At **53** in 2039, with the mortgage nearly paid, I'd feel secure.
I'd plan to be running my **own robot service** well before then.
do: Keep growing the **drone business** and testing tools at Northfield.
**Invest steadily** in the side business and some shares.
Keep **learning new tools** as they appear.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids to be the ones owning a robot, not competing with one.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **fully calm** and optimistic.
Corrects his own **harsh line** about blame when thinking of Gary.
Plans a **steady build** of the side business.
Wants his kids on the **owning side** of robots.

steps.text: Grow the drone business while testing new tools at Northfield
Invest steadily in the side business and some shares
Keep learning each new AI farm tool as it appears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both halves of my job go within three years. What would help is cheap business loans for people setting up robot services, and clear rules so robot makers can't lock out local mechanics. A bit of help for older managers like Gary, too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who fixes the robots. Everyone talks about robots doing the work. A robot in a muddy pig field at 3am breaks down, and somebody local has to go and fix it. I'd like that somebody to be me.

headlineQuote: A robot in a muddy pig field at 3am breaks down, and somebody local has to go and fix it.
portrait: **Marco Hansen**, 43, manages Northfield, a 600-sow **outdoor pig** and grain farm.
He uses **AI every day** and runs a drone crop-scouting business on the side.
He's **calm** in the slow scenarios and sees Steady Disruption as a promotion chance.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious**, because both halves of his manager's job are exposed.
With more warning he'd build a **robot service business** and own the machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both halves of his job go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** for local robot service firms.
Rules stopping robot makers from **locking out** local mechanics.
